newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Gore the big winners of budget deal.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Gore the big winners of budget deal.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and Vice President Al Gore look to be the big winners from the budget agreement but the deal could also help to rescue the Republican-led Congress from their current malaise.
Even though the package was the result of long negotiations with the Republicans and encompasses many prized Republican ideals, Clinton seems likely to take the lion's share of the credit.

"The Republicans could have been winners if they had spent more time claiming credit instead of fighting one another," said former Republican strategist Jack Pitney, now a political scientist at Claremont McKenna College in California.
"But the Republicans are not in a good position to claim credit because they look like the gang that couldn't spin straight. In that sense, they are losers because of what might have been," he said.
In the longer term, anything that benefits Clinton also helps Gore, his designated heir-apparent and the early Democratic frontrunner for the White House in 2000.

Although its fiscal impact looks relatively small, to the extent that the deal helps extends the seven-year economic recovery, Gore could be a big winner too. His future seems inextricably tied to a continuation of the current prosperity.
"If this budget turns out to be good economically, it will be good politically for Gore," said American University political scientist Mark Rozell.
Republicans were especially anxious to wrap up the deal following the abortive attempt by conservatives to unseat House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich earlier this month.

Some conservatives, including potential presidential candidates Jack Kemp and Steve Forbes, are already complaining that Gingrich and Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott made too many concessions to Clinton and there is the potential of the agreement exacerbating Republican splits.

But the Republican leadership had little choice. A budget confrontation with Clinton would only have led to yet another public relations debacle against a president who has repeatedly demonstrated political mastery over them.

"Nobody has denied that President Clinton is glib. He has an ability to frame the issues, and he gets a lot of help from the national news media. We have to try to overcome those," said Lott in a weekend interview.
An agreement -- almost any agreement -- at least gives the Republicans something positive to brag about, even if they have to share the credit with Clinton.

"This is a slight success for Gingrich and the Republicans because they are finally part of something positive. They desperately needed to be affiliated with some kind of victory," said Gregory Valliere of the Washington Research Group which provides political analysis for investors.
Clinton's approval rating, already at historic peaks, may not have much higher to climb. But Gingrich and his colleagues could badly use any kind of popularity boost.

At the same time, House Minority Leader Dick Gephardt, seen as Gore's major Democratic rival for the White House, may emerge the biggest loser. As leader of the party's liberal wing, he opposed many provisions in the deal.

With no major elections until 1998, it is harder to gauge whether or not the deal has a lasting political effect. Some Democrats believe Clinton has stolen many, if not most, of the Republicans' best issues and left his opponents without an effective and unifying agenda.

Others think this kind of bipartisan agreement benefits all incumbents, adding to a sense of public contentment and lack of interest in politics. That would argue for no major threat to Republican control the 1998 congressional elections.

"Republicans should relax. It is their ideas, or a more moderate version of them, that have captured the day. Clinton will retire but their control of Congress seems destined to continue for years to come," said University of Cincinnati political scientist Al Tuchfarber.
